title: Nonequilibrium thermodynamics of feedback-control: a phase-space perspective
abstract: Maxwell demons can convert knowledge into thermodynamic advantage by using measurement-acquired information. However, standard formulations of this problem assume that the demon has access to the system's entire phase space, an assumption that fails in many practical applications. Here, I address this problem by deriving fluctuation relations for general feedback-controlled systems, including such singular cases. The central quantity is a generalized notion of unavailable information: a portion of the acquired information that cannot be used to extract useful work. Finally, a Szilard engine with finite resolution illustrates these results. In the high-resolution limit, the information acquired by the demon may diverge, yet the extractable work remains finite. This work shows that this occurs because an equally divergent amount of information becomes unavailable.
summary: This paper generalizes fluctuation theorems to account for imperfect measurements and feedback control, introducing the concept of 'unavailable information.' By applying this framework to a finite-resolution Szilard engine, it demonstrates that while acquired information can diverge with precision, the extractable work remains bounded by the available information.
main_problem: The work extends fluctuation relations for nonequilibrium processes involving measurement and feedback control, specifically addressing cases where measurements do not have full support over the system's phase space.
main_result: A generalized detailed fluctuation relation is derived, showing that the extractable work in a finite-resolution Szilard engine remains finite even when the acquired information diverges logarithmically with resolution.
method: The derivation uses trajectory probabilities and introduces the concept of 'unavailable information' ($I_u$) to generalize standard fluctuation theorems for singular measurement channels.
model_or_system: The analysis is primarily developed using a stochastic thermodynamic system, exemplified by a Brownian particle in a 1D box undergoing measurements with finite spatial resolution ($\Delta X$).
key_observables: Total entropy production ($S_{tot}$), trajectory transfer entropy ($I_c$), and generalized unavailable information ($I_u$).
important_parameters: Measurement resolution ($\Delta X$) relative to system size ($L$); the ratio $r = \Delta X/L$.
main_assumptions: The standard fluctuation theorem is assumed to fail when measurement channels are singular or lack full support; calculations rely on approximations in the high-resolution limit.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates Maxwell's demon contextually. Figure 2 shows compatible vs. incompatible trajectories restricted by a measurement record. Figure 3 illustrates the Szilard engine with finite spatial resolution $\Delta X$.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the generalized fluctuation relation for feedback systems, then applies this framework to the concrete example of the finite-resolution Szilard engine, deriving explicit formulas for average information and work extraction.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous thermodynamic bound on work extraction that explicitly accounts for measurement limitations (unavailable information), which is crucial for understanding non-ideal quantum measurements or feedback protocols in open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A Maxwell’s demon shines its lantern on particles moving in the dark to gather information about their positions and velocities.

FIG. 2. Examples of trajectories that are compatible (blue) and incompatible (red) with a given measurement record. The colored regions denote the parts of phase space associ- ated with the outcomes obtained during the forward feedback- controlled process. In the backward experiment, the system evolves under the time-reversed protocol but without feed- back, so its intrinsic stochastic dynamics may generate tra- jectories that leave these allowed regions. Such trajectories are incompatible with the original measurement record, as il- lustrated by the red path.
FIG. 3. Szilard engine with spatial resolution ∆X. The de- mon localizes the particle to within one pixel, so decreasing the pixel size allows it to extract more information.
